items.meta_title: Put VpnHood! SERVER Behind a Reverse Proxy Such as Cloudflare | VpnHood!
items.meta_description: Server IP blocked? Put VpnHood! SERVER behind a reverse proxy such as Cloudflare, on a managed server or a standalone one, and know what the proxy sees.
items.title: Put your server behind a reverse proxy
items.lead: A network that blocks your server's IP address stops only the apps that connect to that address. Behind a reverse proxy such as Cloudflare, apps connect to the proxy instead, and the proxy passes the connection on to your server.
items.how_proxy: Your domain leads to the proxy instead of your server. Apps look the domain up and connect to the proxy, which decrypts the connection, as it does for any website it serves, and encrypts it again toward your server. Their traffic goes over WebSocket, which Cloudflare passes on. Another reverse proxy works too, if it passes WebSocket on and reaches your server over TLS; your server then needs its addresses, as Your users' addresses shows.
items.diagram_title: Apps reach your server through the proxy
items.diagram_desc: Your users' apps look up your domain and connect to the reverse proxy, such as Cloudflare, which passes the connection on to your server. The direct route to your server's IP address is blocked, and the apps go around it.
items.diagram_caption: The proxy gets apps past the block
items.how_reach: Apps look the domain up only if their key carries it as a trusted name, which takes a certificate from a certificate authority.
items.how_keys: A key can carry your server's own address as well. Apps then connect either way: the proxy keeps them connected if the address is blocked, but anyone holding the key can read the address. A key without your server's address sends every app through the proxy.
items.limit_block: Blocking: A network can still block the reverse proxy's addresses, or your domain. Cloudflare's addresses serve many other websites, though, so blocking them has a cost.
items.limit_dns: DNS: Apps look your domain up through the network's DNS before they connect. If the network blocks or falsifies the answer, apps fall back to the addresses in their key, so a key that carries only the domain cannot connect.
items.limit_private: Privacy: The reverse proxy sees what is inside the tunnel, just as your server does: where your users connect, and anything they send unencrypted. Their HTTPS stays encrypted. Use a reverse proxy you trust.
items.limit_tcp: TCP only: Your server does not offer its UDP and QUIC ports to apps that come through the proxy.
items.limit_terms: Terms: Check that your provider's terms allow VPN traffic. A small group of users, around 50 or fewer, is usually fine.
items.req_cert: A domain or a subdomain, with a certificate from a certificate authority on your server: Use a domain name and a trusted certificate shows how. Do that first, while the domain's record still points straight at the server.
items.req_one_server: A single server behind the domain. Records that lead to two servers can send the connections of one session to both, and the session breaks.
items.req_port: The server listening on TCP port [server_port], or on another port the proxy passes on. Cloudflare passes HTTPS on [cloudflare_https_ports] only.
items.proxy_record: In Cloudflare, open your domain's DNS records and set the one that points at your server to [cloudflare_proxied], and its AAAA record too if it has one.
items.proxy_ssl: Under [cloudflare_ssl_tls], set the encryption mode to [cloudflare_full_strict]. Cloudflare then reaches your server over TLS and checks its certificate. In [cloudflare_flexible] mode it would use plain HTTP, which the server does not accept.
items.proxy_renew: VpnHood! MANAGER renews its certificates over plain HTTP on TCP port [port_http], through the domain, and Cloudflare passes that on to your server. On a managed server, leave [cloudflare_always_https] off: it would redirect the request to HTTPS, and the renewal would fail.
items.addresses_desc: Behind a proxy, every connection reaches your server from the proxy's address. The proxy names the user's own address in the [header_x_forwarded_for] header, and your server believes that header only from a proxy it trusts, since anyone could write any address in it. Behind a proxy it does not trust, every user seems to connect from the proxy.
items.addresses_cloudflare: Cloudflare: nothing to set. Your server trusts Cloudflare's addresses, which it fetches from Cloudflare when it starts and then daily. It ignores the header in a request from a Cloudflare Worker, though, as anyone can run a Worker that writes any address in it.
items.addresses_cloudfront: Amazon CloudFront: set [setting_reverse_proxy_providers] to [json_providers_cloudfront]. Weigh it first: anyone with an AWS account can run code on CloudFront that writes any address in the header, and your server would believe it.
items.addresses_other: Another proxy: list its addresses in [setting_reverse_proxy_ip_ranges], each a single address or a range such as [ip_range_example], and have the proxy send [header_x_forwarded_for]. Without the header, your server cannot tell that apps come through a proxy, and offers them its UDP and QUIC ports, which lead around the proxy, straight to your server.
items.caption_addresses: A proxy of your own trusted, as well as Cloudflare
items.addresses_none: [setting_reverse_proxy_providers] set to [json_empty_list] trusts no provider, Cloudflare included, and your server then fetches no list.
items.addresses_log: When your server ignores the header, its log names the address that sent it, and why.
items.mgr_box_title: Send every app through the proxy with VpnHood! MANAGER
items.mgr_box_desc: A standalone server always puts its own addresses in its keys. In the free web panel, you take them out with a few clicks, so every app connects through the proxy.
items.file_cert: Check that the server uses the domain's certificate, with [setting_is_valid_host_name] set to [json_true]: Use a domain name and a trusted certificate shows how. Keys made since then carry the domain, and apps look it up.
items.file_keys: A standalone server always puts its own addresses in its keys, beside the domain, so apps use them and the proxy alike. The proxy keeps your users connected when an address is blocked, but anyone holding a key can read the address.
items.file_addresses: If your server needs the settings in Your users' addresses, put them under [setting_file_access_manager] in [server_appsettings], then restart the server.
